newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Rangatira case not a precedent, say commentators.
newsitem.headline: Rangatira case not a precedent, say commentators.

text.p: Treasury, Inland Revenue and lawyers for charity investor Rangatira on Tuesday played down the precedent-setting implications of Rangatira's victory in a Privy Council tax case.
But a taxation expert said the verdict had far-reaching implications for similar cases involving tens of millions of dollars in back taxes.

The British-based Privy Council ruled that Rangatira was not liable to pay tax on capital gains made in the process of buying and selling shares. The company had objected to a $3.8 million tax bill, arguing it was not carrying on a business of buying and selling shares for profit.

The case had been touted by tax experts as precedent-setting because it had gone to the Privy Council but the council simply ruled the Appeal Court was incorrect to overturn the original victory for Rangatira.
However, the ruling is still viewed as a victory for the taxpayer.
"It's good news for taxpayers, particulary for individuals. It reverses a trend that was developing," said Graeme Smaill, a tax partner with law firm Bell Gully which conducted the defence.
The case centred on whether profits on shares bought at low prices and sold at higher prices were taxable.
The five law lords ordered the commissioner of Inland Revenue to pay Rangatira's costs for both the Privy Council appeal and earlier hearings in the Appeal Court and High Court.
Smaill agreed that the case was decided very much on its own facts and noted the Privy Councillors said another judge in the orginal case might have ruled differently.
"I think they are indicating this is pretty finely balanced," he said.
That is the line taken by both Treasury and Inland Revenue.

"It seems the judges have decided the matter basically on the facts of what Rangatira did, rather than being one based on what the law in New Zealand is. So I don't think they have changed the law much," said Treasury's tax director Peter Wilson. He said they had not gone into questions of law.

"The judgement is specific and did not break new ground in clarifying the distinction between capital and revenue, so the implications as a precedential case are not there," said Brian Holland, Inland Revenue's National Manager of Operations Policy.
Smaill said, however, the decision did have significance and could affect billions of dollars of assets.
"The indications were from recent cases that New Zealand companies could be taxable on all their capital gains.
"That's been rejected by the Privy Council. They have said there is a distinction between holding investments and dealing and you have to maintain that distinction.
"If the Privy Council had not reversed the decision, then it could have involved billions of dollars. You are talking about all the capital assets of all New Zealand companies.

"It's not just a matter of reversing the trend that all companies are subject to capital gains tax, it reverses a trend in courts saying 'we are not really interested in the specific reasons for sellling, we are just going to look at the big picture... and if you have done enough over a period of time and we are going to be stringent, then you're a trader'," he said.
Coopers and Lybrand tax partner John Shewan said the decision had far-reaching implications.
"This is a very significant development for the business community," he said.
If the Rangatira decision had gone in favour of Inland Revenue, the "tax net" on capital gains would have been widened considerably, he said.
A number of similar cases involving back taxes -- which had been put on hold -- hinged on the Rangatira decision.
The judgment would affect tens of millions of dollars in back taxes, but in time the sum affected could rise to more than $100 million, he said.
Neither Holland nor Wilson could put a figure on how much in back taxes would be affected or whether the ruling affected forward tax projections.
